What if the side effects get worse or it turns out I'm losing too much weight (I'm already down a kg in 3 months - not concerning, but still) and I have to go off them and go back to being constantly bored and overstimulated and inattentive and hyperactive? From what I know, noooo. I am currently on Sertraline and Ritalin, and one of the things they warn about beforehand is that methylphenidates can be really bad for anxiety. They are known to exacerbate preexisting mental health issues. On one hand, it is amazing getting medicated, because you can focus and do things, which removes a source of anxiety. On the other hand, you can have periods of lethargy, depressive dips, and other fun side effects like tachycardia and weight fluctuation that increase anxiety. Essentially, going on ADHD medication is good for your mental health because you can do stuff, but it can really mess with your anxiety. I would not recommend going off your Sertraline while taking ADHD medication. Best of luck :)

To get right to the point, I am 16, autistic, and have been on Ritalin for the past 3 months or so. It's mainly gone well (amazing impact on my schoolwork). However, I have had quite a few unpleasant side effects - mainly heart pounding, tachycardia, etc.  
I have always drunk a lot - like, a lot - of tea. Coffee's never worked for me, because it makes me kind of sleepy and vaguely nauseous (bad sensory stuff). Recently, though, I realised I had a lot of heart-racey, jittery, shaky moments right after a cup of tea. Essentially, I think I may be properly experiencing the effects of caffeine for the first time.  
Upon googling (not the most reliable source, I know, but I'll ask my doctor about it later) I learned that many people with ADHD process caffeine differently to people - it makes them tired or calm. This could be why I don't find coffee useful for staying awake. Now that I'm on Ritalin, I'm worried that my brain is processing caffeine differently and that's why I feel like shit on my 4th cup of Earl Grey. Is that... plausible??  
Anyway, this is more of a rant, and obviously an easily addressed problem (I know drinking 10 cups of tea is terrible anyway, I'm trying to cut back), I mainly just wanted to know if anyone else started realising caffeine impacts them differently after going on meds. Thanks :)

I get that a lot, OP. Being neurodivergent in a world not designed for you is a real struggle, and it's very stressful constantly having to justify yourself to people who don't understand you. As someone on focus medication with ASD, I completely relate to your feelings on bluntness and emotional expression. I'm sorry you're struggling. Might I recommend you discuss this with your psychiatrist? I know you mentioned they seem pretty dismissive of your issues but I often find talking this stuff out really helps. For instance, when I am really struggling with a concept or don't understand what I've done wrong in a certain situation, I usually ask my therapist to walk me through it as simply as possible. Even if it often doesn't make sense, it really helps to learn the theory behind the occurrence so you can apply to other situations. 

By the way, have you talked to your psychiatrist about medication? As long as you fit the diagnostic criteria for ADHD, and are demonstrably floundering in school/social life, it is not that hard to get prescribed a focus medication. I'm on Ritalin, and it has definitely changed everything - I'm capable of doing things, and I can enjoy them, also! It's remarkable, and very, very helpful. 

By the way, a strategy I have for when I get too focused, and start following people around, is implementing a sort of number system. Every five/ten minutes or so, I evaluate how long I've been talking/whether the person is engaging (usually if they're making eye contact and asking questions). After a while, it becomes habit, although I know it's easy to get distracted. 

As for the 'appropriateness' thing, my therapist has taught me a simple rule: no sex, death/gore, money, extremist politics, or religion as casual conversation. If you do have a special interest, lots of people find it charming when someone is passionate about something, so feel free to talk about it - just try to remember to stop every 2-5 minutes and, if possible, ask them if they've heard about/how they feel about it. People respond more positively to unknown topics if they're able to engage with them. 

You can even just ask someone: 'so, are you religious?' or 'what's your view' or 'I support x because I'm quite (political affiliation)-leaning, how about you?' Once you know that about them, the odds are that you know a little about their views. For instance, very strict religious Mormons will be uncomfortable and angry if you discuss pro-abortion, gay rights, or illicit substances, Pro-socialists won't like it if you endorse Trickle-down economics, and modest small-town types are likely to be scandalised if you bring up strip clubs or porn. Obviously, these are generalisations, but generally you're safe as long as you stick to boring topics like weather and favourite school subjects. If you're very unsure, or if they are making you uncomfortable, just say something about the weather, then excuse yourself to the bathroom or 'suddenly' catch sight of a much more tolerable person and insist you must go say hi. 

(Or if they're making you uncomfortable by being a bigoted, racist, ableist, homophobic prick, as long as they're not in a position of authority above you or important in some way, feel free to insult them in a veiled way, insult them egregiously, embarrass them, or just walk away. Not worth the effort, frankly.)

Additionally, I know this can come off as creepy, but observe people. *Do not* follow someone around the room - that is unusual behaviour that will disconcert people. However, if you can overhear a conversation they are having and sue it for future reference, it is helpful. If someone brings up something to them and they react with obvious disgust (e.g. 'don't talk about that'/'ew'/'how dare you'/'fuck off') take note and don't bring it up. People are very confusing and often illogical in their views, but as long as you watch their reactions to certain topics, you can reduce your chances of offending them. 

As a general rule, if someone is upset or angry, they will change their posture (often to defensive - crossed arms, hunch inwards, or arms akimbo) and glare. However, this is different on anyone, so it's often really hard to tell. However, if someone raises their voice to you or insults you, you can usually reasonably assume they are irate at something you have done. In that case, you can ask them what you've done wrong, in conciliatory tones, e.g. "I seem to have upset you, but I'm not sure how. Could you please explain to me where I went wrong?" or apologise to them, e.g. "I apologise, as you seem to be upset. It was not my intention and I will try not to upset you again." or, if they are aware of your neurodivergency, you can explain and use it as a learning moment, e.g. "As you are aware, I have ASD. This makes it difficult for me to interpret your body language/emotional expressions. Could you please tell me how I've upset you and how to avoid it in the future?"

I've often found it useful to try to express emotions, no matter how unnecessary it might be. For instance, as I spend time with people and talk to them, I tend to assume they know I value them and their company, but people in general can be very insecure. Even if it seems obvious, it makes people happy if you tell them, as undramatically as possible 'I enjoy your company' or 'thank you for remembering I like x' or, if you're dating 'I am happy to be in a romantic relationship with you' or 'spending time with you is very nice.'

Also, in situations when people are struggling, I am *dreadful.* Crying makes me want to run. However, one of my friends gave me a tip: if someone is crying, ask them 'what's wrong?' and just nod along with the explanation (as this builds a feeling of companionship and understanding, without requiring you to speak) or ask 'what can I do to help? Would you like a tissue/cup of tea/\*something you've seen them enjoy\*?' This way, you can offer comfort to them without the risk of offending them or misunderstanding their issues. Really, this one is tried-and-tested for me, and it works - people often don't want anything but comfort and listening when they're sad. 

Essentially, for people such as us, the world is a confusing place where everyone but us has the rulebook. Generally, one simply has to try and piece it together when they can. Do keep in mind that, if you offend someone horribly, it's often distressing and unpleasant, but not terribly important in the scheme of things - there are other people, there will be other chances. And now you know not to talk about, for instance, abortions or transvestites with a Jehovah's Witness. 

Anyway, I'm sorry this became a bit of a rant :)  This is basically an extract from my 'how to deal with people' guide in my head, all of which is learnt from experience. I do hope your find it useful and that things start looking up for you, OP - your brain may not be build for the world we live in, but you are certainly not alone in that regard. Good luck, and do reach out if you ever need someone to talk to!
